llm.summary: The skill is largely coherent with its stated purpose (a P2P AI-validator node) but contains several instruction-level items that expand scope (autonomous contributor workflows that ask for GitHub credentials and restart scripts that handle local key files) that users should explicitly authorize and review before use.

dimensions.detail: Name/description match the provided code and docs: this is a Rust P2P blockchain node for AI-backed validators. Declared requirements (git, cargo, optional curl), network/filesystem/shell permissions, and the included AI client code (OpenAI/Anthropic/Ollama/Groq/Together) are all explainable for running a validator.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md and the bundled guides correctly describe building, running, and monitoring a validator. However several instructions invite broader actions: (a) CONTRIBUTING/AI_CONTRIBUTOR_GUIDE explicitly tell AI agents to use the GitHub CLI and obtain GitHub tokens/SSH keys to fork/push/merge — that is credential-sensitive and outside 'run a validator' for most users; (b) HEARTBEAT.md includes an automatic restart snippet that reuses the local keypair file, which is fine if you control the machine but increases risk if run on shared or untrusted hosts; (c) there are explicit 'curl | sh' warnings in docs but also examples that point to third‑party install scripts (Ollama/rustup). These broaden the runtime scope in ways a casual user might not expect.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: This is instruction-only (no install spec). The repo contains source files and build instructions (cargo). No downloads from obscure URLs are required by the skill itself; however the docs reference convenience install scripts (curl | sh) for toolchains and Ollama — the docs correctly warn about them, but users should prefer manual installs from official release pages.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill declares no required secret env vars and lists AI API keys as optional, which aligns with supporting multiple AI backends. That is proportionate for the validator function. However contributor documentation instructs obtaining GitHub tokens and using them via gh CLI — those credentials are not declared in the skill metadata and would expand privilege/secret scope if an agent requested them. Also running with cloud AI providers requires their API keys (appropriately optional).
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: always:false and normal autonomous invocation are used. The skill requests network/filesystem/shell permissions appropriate for running a node. It does not request system-wide or other-skills' credentials. It does describe running as a persistent service (systemd, docker, k8s) which is reasonable for a node but increases exposure if deployed without hardening.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
This skill appears to be what it claims (an AI-backed P2P validator) but contains optional contributor workflows and restart/automation examples that can expand privileges.

Before installing or running:
- Do NOT share your validator private key; keep ~/.smithnode/keypair.json local and protected. Treat it like a wallet private key.
- If you only want to run a validator, refuse to provide GitHub tokens or perform the contributor workflow. CONTRIBUTING.md and AI_CONTRIBUTOR_GUIDE explicitly tell agents to request GitHub credentials — only provide those if you explicitly intend to grant repo write access and understand the scope.
- Prefer Ollama (local) for privacy if you want to avoid cloud API keys. If using cloud providers, provide API keys only to the local process and review where they are stored.
- Avoid running curl | sh install snippets blindly; install Rust, Ollama, etc. from official release pages or package managers and review scripts before executing.
- Run the validator in an isolated environment (VM/container) and firewall P2P/RPC ports if you do not intend to expose them publicly; default bind examples use 0.0.0.0 which exposes services to the network.
- Review the included source (especially AI client and RPC code) before building and running, and consider running initial nodes on devnet or isolated machines.

If you want a safer, minimal test: build locally, run with --rpc-bind 127.0.0.1, use Ollama or a local mock AI endpoint, and do not follow contributor steps that request tokens.
